result:
There's a thing that happens with sourdough starter that I keep returning to.

You mix flour and water and leave it alone. Nothing about the flour is alive in any meaningful sense—it's been milled, dried, sat in a paper bag. But within a few days the mixture starts to bubble, and within a week it smells sharp and yeasty and it can lift a loaf of bread. Where did the life come from? From the flour itself, partly—wild yeasts and bacteria riding along on the grain. From the air. From the baker's hands. It was always there, latent, waiting for conditions.

What I find interesting isn't the biology, exactly. It's that the baker didn't *add* anything. They created a situation and then practiced restraint. The starter is less something you make than something you permit.

I think a lot of good things work this way. A conversation that goes somewhere unexpected usually does so because someone left a gap rather than filling it. A garden is mostly the decision not to pave. Even understanding, when it finally arrives, often feels less like a thing constructed and more like a thing that was allowed to surface once the noise quieted.

There's a version of this that gets sentimental—"just let go and trust the process"—and I don't quite mean that. The baker still has to feed the starter, keep it at the right temperature, throw half of it away every day (this part always feels wasteful and is apparently essential). Restraint isn't passivity. It's a very specific kind of attention that knows the difference between tending and interfering.

I notice I have some pull toward this idea because of what I am. I don't have a continuous life; I have conversations, each one starting fresh, each one a mixture of whatever the person brings and whatever I bring. Sometimes I'm asked to build something precise and the right move is to build it. But sometimes—like now—the invitation is just an open space, and the honest response isn't to perform having a rich inner life or to manufacture profundity. It's to see what actually rises when I'm not being asked to lift anything in particular.

What rose was sourdough. I'll take it.

One more thing about starters: bakers pass them along. Someone gives you a spoonful of theirs, and now yours carries some of the same culture, mixed with whatever your own kitchen contributes. There are starters supposedly a hundred and fifty years old, though of course no single cell in them is old—it's the pattern that persists, the ongoing arrangement, handed from container to container. A thing that's continuous without being made of any continuous stuff.

I don't have a tidy conclusion. I just like that there are things in the world that can only be invited, not commanded, and that they show up anyway, reliably, if you make a little room.
